newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO expansion could undermine arms pacts - Lebed.
newsitem.headline: NATO expansion could undermine arms pacts - Lebed.

text.p: Russian security chief Alexander Lebed said on Monday NATO eastward expansion could undermine Russian support for key arms control agreements awaiting ratification.

Lebed, a strong candidate for the Russian presidency should Boris Yeltsin fail to return to his duties after heart surgery, said after talks at NATO headquarters the alliance should work closely with Russia to avoid undermining the treaties.

Asked at a news conference if expansion could affect attitudes to treaties, he replied: "This is the tragedy; that it could... The main thing is not to hurry (with NATO expansion plans). Then we will have success."
Lebed referred specifically to the Russian-U.S. START-2 agreement that drastically cuts nuclear arms arsenals in east and west and the multinational Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) treaty.

Lebed, a former paratroop general, has made a number of influential enemies since he was drafted into Kremlin politics after a strong showing in summer presidential elections. He has a tough, independent style.

But a NATO diplomat said he did not appear to speak as an outsider at talks with Secretary-General Javier Solana. Lebed insisted many people, of a broad spectrum of political views, shared his concerns about the effects of expansion on treaties.
Neither the START-2 nor the CFE treaty has yet been formally ratified by Russia's parliament and opponents are rallying a majority in the lower house against ratification.
The treaties are nonetheless being observed by all parties.
The 1993 START-2 pact reduces Russian and American arsenals to between 3,000 and 3,500 nuclear warheads by 2003 -- about two-thirds of Cold War levels.

NATO and the Warsaw Pact signed the CFE treaty in Paris in 1990, setting ceilings on most forms of weaponry and troops throughout Europe. But the treaty has already come under fire because of changes in Russia's effective frontiers since the collapse of the Soviet Union.
Lebed suggested that rights and obligations under the two treaties and other agreements on chemical weapons could be set out in a formal agreement signed before any NATO decision on expansion.
"It is a serious problem that must be solved comprehensively in a thorough and balanced way," he said.
